newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Garzarelli turns positive on U.S. stocks.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Garzarelli turns positive on U.S. stocks.

text.p: Stock market strategist Elaine Garzarelli reversed her bearish position and said she expects a rise of 10 to 15 percent in stocks in the next 12 months.

She said her July call that stocks were due for a fall was incorrect because the most highly-weighted factor in her model had gone sour. But after improvements in other indicators and a recalibration of the errant factor, she is now a bull.
"We see a gain of 10 to 15 percent, assuming no change in interest rates," she said in a telephone interview with Reuters from her Boca Raton, Florida office.

She also said any corrections in this time period should be limited to between four and seven percent. The reading on her new stock market predicting model is 67.5 percent, with anything above 65 percent a bull market signal.
Rumors that Garzarelli, made famous by her accurate prediction of the 1987 stock market meltdown, turned bullish hit the market on Thursday but were not confirmed publicly until now.
On July 22, she turned bearish and called for a correction of 15 to 20 percent. Since then the Dow industrials have soared almost 30 percent.

Some analysts suggested Garzarelli's reversal might have contributed to Thursday's Dow loss of nearly 100 points, because of the widely-held theory that the end of a bullish phase is marked by the capitulation of remaining bears.
"We had trouble with our valuation indicator, which gave us the first incorrect call we've ever had in our career... Since we knew we were wrong, we went back to the drawing board," she said.
The U.S. economy "will be in the bottom of a cycle in the second and third quarter of 1997, after peaking in the first through fourth quarters of 1996," she said.
She said that stocks did not undergo the cyclical downturn in the strong part of the cycle due to good corporate operating earnings and were now insulated from such a fall.

The weakness of the past few days "is a gift ... Get in on the weakness," she said. She said the recent softness in bonds in the past two days was due to fears of a rate hike if coming economic data shows strength.

Garzarelli said the cash flow to short- and long-term rates indicator is no longer being accurately reported by S&P 500 companies. It has been replaced in the model with operating earnings per share to short- and long-term rates.
Garzarelli said her model takes into account no raise in interest rates by the Federal Reserve, 1997 GDP growth of 2.0 to 2.5 percent, and flat corporate earnings by the S&P 500 companies.
"The consensus on corporate earnings is a lot higher so we are being very conservative. If we're being too conservative, there's more upside," she said.
The only monkey wrench that could possibly turn her back into a Cassandra is if the Fed were to raise interest rates by 50 basis points or more.
"Then you could have a greater correction than four to seven percent," Garzarelli said.
Barring that, "since we're bottoming in the economy, we might not get a sell signal for a couple of years," she said.
